sec.title: Case:
sec.p: This is a first report describing preservation of the femoral head by transcervical resection of proximal femoral Ewing sarcoma in 2 pediatric patients. A unique Capanna reconstruction supported joint salvage. At 1 year, Pediatric Outcomes Data Collection Instrument and Pediatric Toronto Extremity Salvage Score outcomes were excellent. Surveillance magnetic resonance imaging was without evidence of recurrence or impaired perfusion to the femoral head.

sec.title: Conclusion:
sec.p: We demonstrate the feasibility of hip joint preservation and maintenance of femoral head viability after transcervical resection of pediatric proximal femur bone sarcomas while preserving the medial circumflex femoral artery. This technique may be a preferred option over joint sacrifice and endoprosthetic replacement in young patients when tumor margins permit.

body.p: Most pediatric bone sarcomas today are treated with chemotherapy and limb salvage surgical resection. When tumors involve the proximal femur, resection commonly requires joint sacrifice and endoprosthetic reconstruction (EPR) with a proximal femoral replacement (PFR). EPRs are fraught with complications that can be magnified in pediatric patients1-4. Pediatric PFR leads to acetabular dysplasia and progressive subluxation of the prosthetic hemiarthroplasty femoral heads5.

Preservation of the native hip joint can mitigate complications associated with pediatric PFR. Modern magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) permits accurate understanding of tumor extent and makes joint-preserving resections feasible6,7. While several reconstructive methods for these intercalary segments exist8-14, extremely short proximal segments limit these options. In addition, femoral head viability requires preservation of the medial circumflex femoral artery (MCFA) during the resection15. We describe 2 cases of proximal femur Ewing sarcoma in pediatric patients treated with joint-preserving resections through the femoral neck reconstructed using bulk allograft plus a vascularized fibular graft (VFG) (Capanna technique).
The patients were informed that data concerning their cases would be submitted for publication, and they provided consent.

sec.title: Case Report
sec.p: The clinical presentations of both patients—a 9-year-old boy (Patient 1) and a 7-year-old girl (Patient 2)—were similar: each presented with progressive proximal thigh pain before diagnosis. Imaging identified an aggressive lesion in the proximal femoral metadiaphysis (Figs. 1-A and 2-A). Biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of Ewing sarcoma, and staging studies ruled out metastatic disease. Conventional neoadjuvant chemotherapy was completed, and post-treatment MRI confirmed the feasibility of femoral head preservation with tumor resection (Figs. 1-B, 1-C and 2-B, 2-C).

caption.p: Fig. 1-A Patient 1 anterior-posterior radiograph exhibiting an aggressive bone tumor with a permeative growth pattern and extensive periosteal reaction in the right proximal femur metadiaphysis. Preoperative T2 MRI coronal (Fig. 1-B) and sagittal (Fig. 1-C) stills demonstrate the extent of the proximal femur Ewing sarcoma after neoadjuvant chemotherapy. MRI = magnetic resonance imaging.

Fig. 2-A Patient 2 anterior-posterior radiograph exhibiting a poorly marginated bone lesion with periosteal reaction in the left proximal femur metadiaphysis. Preoperative T2 MRI coronal (Fig. 2-B) and sagittal (Fig. 2-C) stills after neoadjuvant chemotherapy demonstrate the feasibility of hip joint preservation after resection of the Ewing sarcoma. MRI = magnetic resonance imaging.

sec.p: The surgical technique used in each case was similar. The patient was placed in the lateral decubitus position facilitating a lateral approach to the femur. The vastus lateralis, gluteus sling, and abductors were released off the femur and tagged. The distal femur osteotomy was made with an oscillating saw 2 cm below the tumor according to preoperative MRI measurements. Marrow margins were negative for tumor. The proximal femur was abducted, and all medial insertions of the adductors were carefully released. We protected the profunda femoral artery and descending circumflex branches, clipping vessels as needed to maintain options for microvascular anastomosis. After releasing the psoas tendon, we dissected the MCFA from its origin off the profunda femoris artery to its intracapsular insertion and division into the superior retinacular arteries. We made a T-capsulotomy and could visualize the MCFA arborize into multiple divisions entering the femoral neck (Fig. 3). A wire was placed into the proximal physis under fluoroscopic guidance, and a saw was used to cut just distal and parallel to this wire giving us a minimum 1 cm margin proximally. The specimen was removed, and the proximal marrow margin was negative (Fig. 4). At no point was the femoral head dislocated from the acetabulum. The microvascular team harvested the ipsilateral VFG according to described techniques16.

caption.p: Intraoperative photograph of the MCFA (white arrowhead) dissected to its insertion into the hip joint capsule in Patient 1. The femoral neck osteotomy has been performed in situ while protecting this vessel and its proximal branches. MCFA = medial circumflex femoral artery.
Intraoperative frozen section margins were negative for tumor. A gross pathology hemisection of the resected specimen confirmed this postoperatively.

sec.p: A thawed, size-matched femoral allograft (MTF Biologics) was cut to match the resection specimen (Fig. 5-A). We placed a long proximal humerus locking plate (DePuy Synthes) on the lateral aspect of the reconstruction and placed guidewires through the allograft into the posterior aspect of the native femoral head ensuring adequate screw fixation while leaving room for the vascularized fibula (Fig. 5-B). After returning the graft to the back table, a burr was used to create a trough in which the VFG could be inserted using an in-lay technique (Fig. 5-C). An osteotomy was made in the VFG, recreating the neck-shaft angle, preserving the periosteal blood supply to the distal strut16. The fibula extended 1 cm beyond the length of the allograft at each end so that it could intussuscept into host bone. The lateral plate and screw fixation was then reapplied to the Capanna reconstruction in vivo. An orthogonal mini-fragment plate (Synthes) was applied to the distal junction for rotational control (Fig. 6, Video 1). The microvascular team then performed the anastomosis between the peroneal vessels and the lateral femoral circumflex system. After closing the T-capsulotomy, we rotated the proximal thigh musculature back into position obtaining good soft-tissue coverage over the allograft and sewed the abductors through the plate into the greater trochanter. The wound was closed in layers (Figs. 7-A and 7-B).

caption.p: Intraoperative photograph of the allograft (left) cut to match the resection specimen (right). Fig. 5-B A trough was created in the allograft, and the VFG was osteotomized to match the neck-shaft angle. Plate fixation was applied avoiding the VFG pedicle (Fig. 5-C). The final Capanna reconstruction using an in-lay technique. VFG = vascularized fibular graft.

Photograph of the final reconstruction in Patient 1 with the vascular anastomosis visible anterior to the allograft. A small fragment plate was placed posteriorly for added rotational control of the distal junction.

An intraoperative video of the Capanna reconstruction in Patient 2 demonstrating intussusception of the VFG into the native femoral head, proximally, and femoral canal, distally, with lateral plate fixation along the bulk allograft.

Patient 1 two-week postoperative anterior-posterior (Fig. 7-A) and lateral (Fig. 7-B) radiographs demonstrate the proximal subcapital and distal diaphyseal osteotomies bridged by the allograft-VFG Capanna construct reconstituting anatomic alignment of the femur. VFG = vascularized fibular graft.

sec.p: The patient was made non–weight-bearing and fitted for a hip abduction brace, always worn except when in bed. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy resumed within 3 weeks of surgery. Progressive weight-bearing was initiated 3 months postoperatively. The allograft junctions healed by 6 months, and he was able to walk independently with a Trendelenburg gait. At 1 year, radiographs demonstrated further maturation of both osteotomy sites and, crucially, no evidence of femoral head avascular necrosis (AVN) (Figs. 8-A, 8-B and 8-C and 9-A through 9-D). Surveillance MRI scans were without evidence of local recurrence, nor any signal abnormality indicating impaired perfusion to the femoral head. Functional outcomes surveys including the adolescent (parent-reported) version of the Pediatric Outcomes Data Collection Instrument (PODCI) and the self-reported Pediatric Toronto Extremity Salvage Score (pTESS) were administered and were excellent (Table I). Abductor deficiency substantially improved at 1.5 years postoperatively, and he was cleared for noncontact sports participation.

caption.p: One-year follow-up images for Patient 1. Fig. 8-A and lateral (Fig. 8-B) radiographs demonstrate full healing of the proximal and distal host-allograft junctions. The femoral head has retained viability and sphericity within a normal-appearing acetabulum. The long-leg standing radiograph (Fig. 8-C) demonstrates anatomic limb alignment and a minor leg length discrepancy.

One-year follow-up images for Patient 2 exhibit similar allograft healing with femoral head preservation in anterior-posterior (Fig. 9-A), lateral (Fig. 9-B and 9-C) and long-leg (Fig. 9-D) radiographs.
Functional Outcome Scores for Patient 1 One Year Postoperatively as Measured by the PODCI and pTESS

fn.p: PODCI = Pediatric Outcomes Data Collection Instrument, and pTESS = Pediatric Toronto Extremity Salvage Score.
Global function scale = mean of the 4 core physical function scales.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: We report 2 cases of transcervical resections of proximal femur Ewing sarcoma in pediatric patients maintaining viability of the native hip joint after preserving the MCFA and its branches. The intercalary Capanna reconstruction demonstrated radiographic incorporation at both osteotomy locations in each case, and the outcome scores at 1 year were excellent as measured by the PODCI and pTESS for a single case assessed. We suggest this technique be considered in any pediatric proximal femur sarcoma case, in which wide proximal margins can be obtained while preserving the epiphysis and the MCFA in centers with microvascular expertise. It is not suitable for cases in which the tumor extends to the epiphysis or when the MCFA is sacrificed or injured.

Endoprostheses are the most common method of reconstruction after pediatric bone tumor resection4,17. EPRs allow modularity, durability, and immediate weight-bearing, and some systems offer extensible “growing” implants. Unfortunately, PFRs in pediatric patients have demonstrated even higher overall failure rates than their adult counterparts, typically secondary to aseptic loosening and infection1,18. The lengthening mechanism of the extendible implants can also fail19. In a recent meta-analysis, only 52% of extendible pediatric PFRs were actually lengthened for an average of only 3 cm, and 25% of treated patients still had a leg length discrepancy18. Thus, while EPRs can result in excellent functional outcomes for patients, their complication profile remains high3,20.

Resection of the native femoral head impairs acetabular development21, and the presence of a prosthetic femoral head exerts a dysplastic effect on the developing acetabulum. Manoso et al. reported on 8 pediatric patients with osteosarcoma who underwent PFR with a hemiarthroplasty. The expected deepening of the juvenile acetabulum failed to occur, and all patients developed progressive superior and lateral migration of the prosthesis5. Furthermore, a larger study reported a 75% rate of acetabular revision at 10 years, while emphasizing the inability of salvage periacetabular osteotomy procedures to prevent prosthesis subluxation22.

The challenge of hip joint preservation after tumor resection lies in the reconstruction of these intercalary defects having very short proximal segments. The original technique combining a VFG with a bulk allograft (BA) in the leg was described by Capanna in an effort to improve construct biology and resistance to the typical modes of BA failure: infection, fracture, and nonunion10,11,23,24. Overall survival of these reconstructions has proven excellent9,25. The advent of computer navigation, computer-assisted design/computer-assisted manufacturing technologies, and 3D printing can also facilitate narrow-margin, joint-preserving surgeries. Although this remains uncommon in practice, early reports are promising and could have been an option in our cases, too14.

While transphyseal resections have been reported for tumors about the knee7,26, a commensurate technique for tumors of the proximal femur with preservation of the MCFA has not been reported. This is also the first case to apply the principles of a “double-barrel fibula” as originally described16 to support preservation of the femoral head. While prior “double-barrel” studies have described femoral diaphyseal, distal femoral, and tibial reconstructions27-30, this is the first report of the technique applied to reconstruction of the neck-shaft angle. A single prior report using a fibular epiphyseal transfer within bulk allograft attempted to preserve the femoral head as a cap but exhibited AVN and articular collapse within 9 months postoperatively.31

The PODCI includes 4 physical component core scales and a global functioning scale with standardized scores ranging from 0 (worst) to 100 (best function or least pain). A score of 85 is considered the lower limit of normal32. The pTESS is a validated tool for self-reported physical function in pediatric patients with bone tumors33,34. Our patient’s function was excellent in 4 of 5 PODCI scales. His global functioning scale score of 95 was superior to that reported in a cohort of pediatric patients treated with expandable PFRs (79 ± 5)3. Our patient’s pTESS score of 81 mimics the mean score reported by Piscione et al. in their pTESS validation study in pediatric patients with sarcoma (78 ± 16), although those study patients were generally older than our patient and were assessed >2 years from surgery.

In conclusion, we report salvage of the pediatric hip in 2 cases by transcervical resection of a proximal femoral Ewing sarcoma and an intercalary Capanna reconstruction. Preservation of the MCFA was critical to long-term viability of the native femoral head. Additional factors critical to success were accurate preoperative assessment of tumor extent, stable allograft fixation avoiding the VFG pedicle, and application of the “double-barrel” fibula osteotomy. We expect this to be a durable and stable reconstruction optimizing chances for normal acetabular development. Functional outcomes may improve with time as muscular strength improves. Long-term follow-up is needed to evaluate hip development and the suitability of this reconstruction for unrestricted physical activity.
